content.intro: This lesson covers Understanding Result<T, E>. It sits in Module 10, Error Handling, and builds toward a practical Rust mental model rather than memorizing a term in isolation.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding Result<T, E> matters when you work with explicit absence and failure paths. Understanding the rule helps you predict compiler or runtime behavior, document assumptions, and choose a safer implementation when inputs or system conditions change.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Result<T, E> represents either success (Ok(value)) or failure (Err(error)). Callers can handle an error, propagate it with ?, or deliberately convert it.

content_blocks.title: A reliable way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: For Understanding Result<T, E>, write down the inputs, the guarantee you expect, and the boundary where that guarantee stops. Work through a minimal example first; then deliberately test one edge case. Expected failures should normally be represented by Result. Use ? only in a function whose return type can represent the propagated error.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not assume Understanding Result<T, E> guarantees more than it actually does. Reduce a failure to a small reproducer, read the full compiler diagnostic or error value, consult the matching official reference, and change one assumption at a time.
